opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a fairly natural thing to happen when you have a technology that's moving quickly and that people don't fully understand. Policymakers are being asked to regulate something abstract, and the bioweapon story is very concrete. It's easy to picture and it's frightening, so it cuts through in a way that "models might be misused in some diffuse way" never would.

There was also a lot of effort by certain groups, some sincerely worried and some with other incentives, to put that scenario in front of governments early. If you're a policymaker and credible-sounding people walk in with a demo where a chatbot appears to explain something dangerous, that sticks.

When you look closely, though, the evidence for meaningful uplift has been pretty thin. The studies that tried to measure whether a language model helps someone get further than they could with a search engine and a textbook mostly found marginal differences. The hard part of building a biological weapon was never information. It's the wet-lab work: materials, equipment, tacit know-how, and the many steps where things fail. A model that summarizes papers doesn't change that bottleneck much.

So my view is that it gained traction because it's a compelling narrative, not because it was the best-supported risk. The danger is that it pulls regulation toward things like restricting open models or capping compute, which concentrates the technology in a few hands without actually addressing the real chokepoints. If you care about biosecurity, the better approach is to control access to synthesis, reagents, and labs. That's where it's actually tractable, and it's where governments already have tools.

We should take misuse seriously and evaluate our models for it, and we do. But policy should follow evidence, and on this one the story ran ahead of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to look at where it came from. The narrative didn't originate in the biology community. It came mostly from a small number of labs, and from a fairly tight ecosystem of think tanks and funders who had been thinking about existential risk for a long time before large language models existed. When the models arrived, that community already had the framing ready, and the models became the vector for a story that had been waiting for a technology to attach itself to.

And the story is very effective rhetorically, because it combines two things policymakers respond to. One is a vivid worst case: a lone actor, a pandemic, millions dead. The other is a claim of asymmetry: that the information advantage the model provides is decisive. If you put those together, you get something that is very hard for a regulator to say no to. Nobody wants to be the person who dismissed the pandemic risk.

What was missing, in my view, was the question of marginal uplift. The bottleneck for biological weapons has historically not been knowledge. It has been materials, equipment, tacit skills, the actual wet lab work. Most of what a model can tell you is in textbooks and in papers that are already public. So the right question was always: how much does the model add compared to a search engine and a graduate student? And for a long time that question was not really asked. The conclusion was assumed and the evidence came afterwards.

In Europe there was an additional dynamic, which is that a few American companies were very present in Brussels and in national capitals, and they were presenting these risks at the same time as they were proposing the regulatory response. And the regulatory response, conveniently, tended to favour large closed players, because it required capabilities to be gated behind an API, with monitoring and evaluations that only a few organisations could afford. So you had a safety argument that was also a market structure argument, and the two were never really separated in the public discussion.

I don't want to say the risk is zero. We do evaluations on this, and I think everybody serious does. But I think the way it gained traction says more about the sociology of the policy world than about the biology. A dramatic narrative, delivered by credible people with a lot of resources, to policymakers who had very few independent technical advisers. That's a recipe for a story to travel faster than the evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two separate questions: how serious the risk is, and why that particular narrative became so influential. On the second, it’s a very concrete, frightening scenario. You can explain it to a policymaker in thirty seconds, whereas explaining the capabilities and limitations of a model takes much longer.

There’s also an asymmetry of expertise. Policymakers depend on the people developing these systems to explain what might happen. When those people raise a catastrophic possibility, understandably, it gets attention. But we should distinguish a plausible scenario from evidence that a model materially increases someone’s ability to carry it out.

For me, that’s the question policy should focus on: what additional capability does the model provide, and would the proposed restriction actually reduce the risk? You can take the concern seriously while still asking for a much more rigorous connection between the threat and the policy response.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that it’s a very concrete story about a technology that is otherwise quite difficult to understand. If you’re a policymaker, the idea that AI could help someone develop a biological weapon gives you an immediate reason to pay attention. And when that concern comes from people building the technology, it carries weight.

But I would distinguish the plausibility of a risk from evidence about how much AI actually increases it. What could someone do without the model? What additional capability does the model give them? And what practical barriers would still remain? Those are the questions you need to answer to make good policy.

So I wouldn’t dismiss the concern. But I think the narrative can move faster than the evidence, and we should be careful about turning a compelling scenario into the assumption on which we regulate everything.
